title: The Surgeon Who Invented Cesarean Survival
event_summary: In 1879, British medical missionary Robert Felkin witnessed a Ugandan healer in the kingdom of Bunyoro perform a successful cesarean section on a young woman using banana wine as both antiseptic and anesthetic, cauterizing the wound with heated iron, and closing the incision with iron needles and bark-cloth bandages. The mother and child both survived and recovered fully. At the time, cesarean sections in Europe still carried mortality rates above 80 percent, and European surgeons had not yet mastered the combination of antisepsis, anesthesia, and wound closure that this indigenous practitioner demonstrated with local materials.
why_forgotten: Colonial-era European medicine refused to acknowledge that African surgical traditions could be more advanced than their own practices. Felkin published his account in the Edinburgh Medical Journal in 1884, but it was treated as a curiosity rather than a source of legitimate medical knowledge. The systematic erasure of African intellectual and scientific achievement during the scramble for Africa ensured the observation was buried in obscurity.
why_it_matters: This event demonstrates that sophisticated surgical knowledge existed in precolonial Africa independent of European medical traditions, challenging persistent myths about the origins of modern medicine. The Bunyoro technique's integration of antisepsis, pain management, and careful wound closure anticipated principles that European surgeons would not reliably combine until the late 1880s and 1890s. Today, as cesarean sections save millions of lives annually, acknowledging this history reshapes our understanding of who contributed to global medical progress.
